sentences.text: We start at the top left cell, value 1.
Our current direction is right.
We move across the complete top row, from 1 through 6.
At 6, the next position to the right is outside the matrix, so we turn clockwise, from right to down.
Now we move down the complete right edge, from 12 through 30.
At 30, the next downward position is outside the matrix, so we turn from down to left.
Now we move across the bottom edge, from 29 through 25.
At 25, the next position to the left is outside the matrix, so we turn from left to up.
Now we move upward along the left edge until we reach 7.
And here, something different happens.
The cell above 7 is still inside the matrix, but it contains one, and one was already visited.
So this time, we are not turning because of the border, we are turning because the next cell is already visited.
We turn clockwise, from up to right.
This is the important point that lets us enter the inner spiral.
Now we move right, from 8 through 11.
At 11, the next cell is 12.
12 is already visited, so we turn from right to down.
Now we move down until 23.
At 23, the next cell below is 29.
29 is already visited, so we turn from down to left.
Now we move left until 20.
At 20, the next cell is 19.
19 is already visited, so we turn from left to up.
Moving upward, we reach 14.
The cell above 14 is 8.
8 was already visited, so we turn from up to right.
Now only the final two cells remain, 15 and 16.
After adding 16, the answer contains exactly 30 values, and the matrix contains 5 times 6, which is also 30 cells.
So every cell has been visited exactly once, and we stop.
So method 1 always follows the same logic.
Process the current cell, inspect the next position, and turn when that next position is outside or already visited.
Now let's map this exact trace into code.
